Cape Nome data walkthrough: the layers, the model, and the results

A layer-by-layer tour of the inputs and outputs behind the Cape Nome placer and lode prospectivity models. Private working notebook, not linked from the public site.

A hands-on tour of the data feeding the Cape Nome district models, in the same shape as the Tanacross and BC Golden Triangle data-exploration notebooks: one section per layer, each with a rendered map, a note on what the layer is and what it is for, and a note on how the model reads it. The last sections turn to the outputs, the prospectivity surfaces and the cross-validation numbers behind them.

This is a working notebook. It is not in _quarto.yml and is not linked from the public site; it is the place to see every layer at once and decide later what belongs in the public chapter and what belongs in a deeper write-up.

Code 
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import json
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import rioxarray

from ai_minerals.data._common import DATA_RAW, DATA_DERIVED

WORKING_CRS = "EPSG:3338"          # NAD83 Alaska Albers, the district grid CRS
NP = DATA_DERIVED / "nome_placer"
NG = DATA_DERIVED / "nome_geophys"
RM = DATA_RAW / "nome_mpm"
STRUCT = NG / "nome_structure_sharp" / "district_100m"

LODE_SERVED = NP / "mpm_lode_served" / "mpm_lode_served_district_3338.tif"
PLACER_SERVED = NP / "mpm_onshore" / "mpm_onshore_score_district_3338.tif"

print("district CRS:", WORKING_CRS, "(NAD83 Alaska Albers Equal Area)")
print("served lode raster present:  ", LODE_SERVED.exists())
print("served placer raster present:", PLACER_SERVED.exists())
district CRS: EPSG:3338 (NAD83 Alaska Albers Equal Area)
served lode raster present:   True
served placer raster present: True
Code 
def _load(path):
    """Read a single-band raster to a masked float array + its 3338 extent."""
    da = rioxarray.open_rasterio(path).squeeze()
    arr = da.values.astype("float64")
    nod = da.rio.nodata
    if nod is not None and np.isfinite(nod):
        arr = np.where(arr == nod, np.nan, arr)
    arr = np.where(np.isfinite(arr), arr, np.nan)
    left, bottom, right, top = da.rio.bounds()
    return arr, (left, right, bottom, top)

def panel(ax, path, title, cbar_label, cmap="viridis", q=(2, 98),
          mask_neg=False, categorical=False, points=None, pcolor="#ff2d2d",
          psize=16, plabel="occurrences"):
    """Draw one raster on ax, optionally with occurrence points overlaid."""
    arr, extent = _load(path)
    if mask_neg:
        arr = np.where(arr < 0, np.nan, arr)
    if categorical:
        im = ax.imshow(arr, cmap=cmap, extent=extent, origin="upper",
                       interpolation="nearest", aspect="equal")
    else:
        lo, hi = np.nanpercentile(arr, q)
        im = ax.imshow(arr, cmap=cmap, vmin=lo, vmax=hi, extent=extent,
                       origin="upper", interpolation="nearest", aspect="equal")
    cb = plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.82)
    cb.set_label(cbar_label, fontsize=8)
    cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    if points is not None and len(points):
        ax.scatter(points.geometry.x, points.geometry.y, s=psize, c=pcolor,
                   edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.35,
                   label=f"{plabel} (N={len(points)})")
        ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=7, framealpha=0.9)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m, EPSG:3338)", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m)", fontsize=8)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    return arr, extent

def _ardf():
    return gpd.read_file(RM / "ardf_nome.geojson").to_crs(WORKING_CRS)

def _clip(g, extent):
    if extent is None:
        return g
    left, right, bottom, top = extent
    return g.cx[left:right, bottom:top]

def lode_36a(extent=None):
    """ARDF occurrences typed Cox-Singer 36a (low-sulfide Au-quartz vein)."""
    g = _ardf()
    g = g[g["model_code"].fillna("").str.contains("36a", case=False)]
    return _clip(g, extent)

def placer_occ(extent=None):
    """ARDF placer occurrences (commodity names placer, or model code 39x)."""
    g = _ardf()
    comm = (g["comm_main"].fillna("") + " " + g["comm_other"].fillna("")).str.lower()
    code39 = g["model_code"].fillna("").str.strip().str.startswith("39")
    g = g[comm.str.contains("placer") | code39]
    return _clip(g, extent)

def load_json(path):
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text())

The experiment

Two deposit types share this ground. Placer gold is the loose gold in the gravels, the Nome beaches and creek bottoms that the 1899 rush was built on. Lode gold is the hard-rock source: gold-bearing quartz veins in the bedrock that the placer gold weathered out of and washed down from. The project builds a separate prospectivity surface for each, a map that ranks every cell in the district by how favorable it is for that deposit type, trained on the recorded occurrences.

The ruler for both is the same. Every claim a model makes is checked under leak-guarded spatial cross-validation: hold out whole regions of the map, train on the rest, score the held-out occurrences, and pool the out-of-fold predictions into a single area-under-the-ROC-curve (AUC). The frame is presence/background: the positives are recorded occurrences, the negatives are a sample of the district at large rather than known-barren ground, so the model learns what separates occurrence sites from the district average. The point of the discipline is to make a number mean something before reporting it.

Data layers

Each layer below is shown on the 100 m district grid (EPSG:3338), the resolution the regional models run at. The native sources are finer (the IfSAR elevation is 5 m, the LiDAR is 1 m); they are resampled to 100 m here so every covariate sits on one grid.

Terrain: IfSAR elevation, slope, and topographic position

Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
panel(axes[0], RM / "ifsar_dem_district_3338.tif",
      "IfSAR elevation (DEM)", "m above sea level", cmap="terrain")
panel(axes[1], RM / "ifsar_slope_district_3338.tif",
      "Slope", "degrees", cmap="magma")
panel(axes[2], RM / "ifsar_tpi_district_3338.tif",
      "Topographic position index", "TPI", cmap="RdBu_r")
plt.tight_layout()

What it is. The Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (IfSAR) digital elevation model is Alaska’s statewide 5 m radar elevation surface. Slope and the topographic-position index (how high a cell sits relative to its surroundings) are derived from it.

What it is for. Terrain is the backbone of the placer model: the beaches, benches, and creek bottoms where placer gold concentrates have distinct elevation and slope signatures. It is also the feature that made the first lode model lie, because in a small box the lodes sit up in the schist hills and the background sits down on the coastal flat, so a model can separate them on elevation alone and never learn any geology. That trap is the subject of the lode-results section below.

How the model reads it. Elevation, slope, and topographic position enter both models directly as per-cell covariates.

Geology: Nome Group units and the graphitic host

Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
lodes = lode_36a()
panel(axes[0], NP / "covariates_mpm" / "geology_unit_code_district_3338.tif",
      "Surface geology unit", "unit code", cmap="tab20",
      categorical=True, mask_neg=True)
panel(axes[1], STRUCT / "struct_carbonaceous_host.tif",
      "Graphitic / carbonaceous host flag", "host present", cmap="cividis",
      points=lodes, plabel="36a lode")
plt.tight_layout()

What it is. The surface-geology unit at each cell, and a flag for the graphitic (carbon-rich) schists of the Nome Group. The units come from the statewide compilation; the graphitic-host flag comes from the detailed Alaska state maps of the Seward Peninsula bedrock (DGGS SIM 3131 for the Nome and Solomon quadrangles, RI 2024-7 for Casadepaga), which label the carbonaceous units explicitly.

What it is for. The Nome Group schists are the reactive host rock for the gold-quartz veins. Orogenic gold of this type favors carbon-rich units, where the chemistry of the wall rock helps drop gold out of solution. The 36a lode occurrences (red) cluster on and near the graphitic ground.

How the model reads it. The geology unit enters as a set of one-hot indicator columns; the graphitic-host flag enters as its own binary covariate.

Structure: the fault sets, the named faults, and the Groves features

Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
ext = None
for ax, fn, title in [
    (axes[0], "struct_dist_splay.tif", "Distance to a second-order splay"),
    (axes[1], "struct_dist_fault_intersection.tif", "Distance to a NE x NW fault intersection"),
    (axes[2], "struct_dist_fold_hinge.tif", "Distance to a fold hinge"),
]:
    arr, ext = panel(ax, STRUCT / fn, title, "metres", cmap="viridis_r")
lodes = lode_36a(ext)
for ax in axes:
    ax.scatter(lodes.geometry.x, lodes.geometry.y, s=14, c="#ff2d2d",
               edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.35, label=f"36a lode (N={len(lodes)})")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=7, framealpha=0.9)
plt.tight_layout()

What it is. Three structural-distance fields, brighter where the structure is nearer. A second-order splay is a small fault branching off a main fault trunk; an intersection is where a northeast-trending fault crosses a northwest-trending one; a fold hinge is the axis where folded rock layers bend. All three are read from the most detailed public structural map of the district, the Alaska state GeMS geodatabase for the Nome mining district (DGGS PDF 94-39), which also names the district faults: Anvil, Penny River, Aurora Creek, Charlie Creek, Boulder Creek, Rodine.

What it is for. This is the lode model’s centerpiece. Distance to the nearest big fault, the obvious feature, is the wrong one for orogenic gold. Groves and coauthors showed across many districts that the gold does not sit on the fault trunks; it sits in the second-order splays, at the intersection nodes, and near fold hinges, inside the reactive host. Building those controls directly, rather than distance-to-any-fault, is what separated the rebuilt lode model from the failed first version.

How the model reads it. Splay proximity, intersection proximity, and fold-hinge distance enter as three covariates. The results section shows that these are the three features the model leans on hardest, ahead of any individual named fault.

Geophysics: aeromagnetics and 1993 airborne resistivity

Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
panel(axes[0], NP / "covariates_mpm" / "akmag_district_3338.tif",
      "Aeromagnetic field", "nT (stretched)", cmap="RdBu_r")
panel(axes[1], NG / "dighem1993" / "district_100m" / "dighem_res_log10_900hz.tif",
      "1993 DIGHEM apparent resistivity (900 Hz)", "log10 ohm-m", cmap="Spectral_r")
plt.tight_layout()

What it is. The regional aeromagnetic field (magnetic susceptibility of the rocks) and the 1993 Nome DIGHEM-V helicopter electromagnetic survey (DGGS GPR 2019-11, 400 m flight lines), reduced to apparent electrical resistivity. The resistivity covers only the flown strip, so much of the district is blank.

What it is for. The two geophysical layers part ways for the lode, so it is worth separating them. The magnetics carry no independent lode signal once you score them on the flown cells: the marginal AUC is negative, not zero (about -0.02 in the central box, -0.06 district-wide), and the apparent gain on the full extent is coverage, not geology. The DIGHEM apparent resistivity is the one layer that helps at all, and only a little: a small positive at district scale on the flown cells (marginal AUC about +0.03), null in the smaller central box. Tested together the two add about +0.06 in the central box, but the bootstrap interval grazes zero in every case, and neither DIGHEM layer is in the served surface. What carries the lode is structure, not geophysics (the Groves structural features add +0.11 district-wide, P(Δ>0)=0.999).

An expected cross-check also failed. The graphitic units, predicted to read as electrical conductors (a low apparent resistivity, the alteration signature the literature looks for), instead read as more resistive than their surroundings: median apparent resistivity about 0.3 to 0.8 log10 ohm-m higher across the 900 Hz, 7.2 kHz, and 56 kHz channels. We did not test why. One untested possibility is that a 400 m airborne EM survey over permafrost terrain does not resolve deep graphite, but we cannot cite that, so it is a hypothesis, not a finding. Either way the host flag earns its place as a map-geology covariate, not as a geophysical conductor.

What we did not build. We tested these layers one at a time. We did not construct the combined alteration index the literature advocates (low magnetic susceptibility with low apparent resistivity and a localized gravity low, read together as a proxy for a buried hydrothermal center), and gravity is not in the Nome stack at all. The geophysics result here is a limit of what we built, not a refutation of that index.

How the model reads it. The statewide aeromagnetic field enters the served lode model as a base covariate, where it ranks low in feature importance; on placer it is negative. The DIGHEM survey and gravity are not in the served surfaces.

Placer layers: the strandlines, the populations, and the LiDAR

Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
placers = placer_occ()
panel(axes[0], RM / "ifsar_dem_district_3338.tif",
      "Coastal terrain (placer setting)", "m above sea level",
      cmap="terrain", points=placers, plabel="placer occ", pcolor="#00d0ff")
panel(axes[1], NP / "beachline_rem" / "rem.tif",
      "Relative elevation model (1 m LiDAR, coastal strip)",
      "m above local base", cmap="RdYlBu_r")
plt.tight_layout()

What it is. The coastal terrain with the placer occurrences on it (left), and a relative elevation model (right) built from the 2021 NOAA/USACE 1 m bare-earth LiDAR, which detrends the regional slope to make low relief stand out. The Nome placers sit on a stack of raised and submerged paleo-shorelines: the Second Beach at about +38 ft, the Third Beach at +70 ft (the high-grade exemplar), the Fourth at +120 ft, and several submerged stands offshore.

What it is for. These layers encode where the gold-bearing beaches and their reworked stream placers are. The placer model is, in effect, a beach-line model already: its existing features score nearness to a true beach-stand elevation, the abrasion platforms, and the buried beach lines. A round-2 test added the 1 m LiDAR strandline geometry and found it added nothing measurable over that existing backbone, which says the beach-line geometry was the model’s spine all along. The 1 m LiDAR’s real value is berm-scale targeting on a single claim, not district-scale ranking.

How the model reads it. The placer model carries explicit geomorphic population features (beach, abrasion platform, buried beach, stream reworking) on top of the terrain stack.

Labels: the typed lode set and the placer occurrences

Code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
arr, ext = panel(ax, RM / "ifsar_dem_district_3338.tif",
                 "Recorded occurrences over district terrain",
                 "m above sea level", cmap="Greys")
lo = lode_36a(ext); pl = placer_occ(ext)
ax.scatter(pl.geometry.x, pl.geometry.y, s=18, c="#00b3ff", edgecolor="black",
           linewidth=0.3, label=f"placer occ (N={len(pl)})")
ax.scatter(lo.geometry.x, lo.geometry.y, s=26, c="#ff2d2d", edgecolor="black",
           linewidth=0.3, marker="^", label=f"36a lode (N={len(lo)})")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9)
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"36a lode occurrences shown: {len(lo)}   placer occurrences shown: {len(pl)}")
36a lode occurrences shown: 59   placer occurrences shown: 210

What it is. The training labels. The lode positives are the ARDF occurrences the USGS classifies as Cox-Singer model 36a, low-sulfide gold-quartz vein, the deposit type the Nome lodes actually are. The placer positives are the ARDF placer occurrences inside the area of interest.

What it is for. The typed lode set is the other half of the lode fix. The first model used a keyword grab (anything tagged lode or vein), which piled the positives into the two or three most-prospected spots. The 36a type code is assigned from a deposit’s own character, not its location, so the positives disperse across the district and take the elevation shortcut away. The headline label counts the models train on are 65 placer and 54 typed lode occurrences (48 of the lode set fall on GeMS-mapped ground); the counts drawn here come straight from the ARDF file and track those.

How the model reads it. Positives are the occurrence cells; negatives are a background sample of the district. No occurrence-derived feature is allowed to leak the label, which is the subject of the next section.

How the algorithm consumes the data

The covariates above feed a random forest (300 trees, class-balanced, fixed seed), but the modeling choice that decides whether the numbers mean anything is the cross-validation, not the estimator.

Code 
sc = boot["scheme"]
print("Leak-guarded spatial cross-validation:")
print(f"  fold strategy     : {sc['fold_strategy']} regions")
print(f"  number of folds   : {sc['n_folds']}")
print(f"  block size        : {sc['block_size_m']:.0f} m  "
      f"(2x the {sc['variogram_range_m']:.0f} m residual-variogram range)")
print(f"  dead-zone buffer  : {sc['dead_zone_m']:.0f} m around every held-out point")
Leak-guarded spatial cross-validation:
  fold strategy     : contiguous regions
  number of folds   : 10
  block size        : 3800 m  (2x the 1879 m residual-variogram range)
  dead-zone buffer  : 1000 m around every held-out point

Spatial blocks, not random folds. Occurrences cluster, and nearby cells share terrain, so a random train/test split lets the model score a test point off its own near-neighbor in training. The folds here are contiguous regions, sized from the range of spatial autocorrelation in the model’s own residuals (a variogram fit), so a held-out block is large enough to be genuinely independent of the training ground.

A dead-zone around every test point. On top of the block split, any training cell within 1 km of a held-out occurrence is dropped, which is wider than the few-hundred-meter proximity buffers in the structural features. A test point cannot be scored by a training neighbor sitting just across the fold line.

The leakage lesson. An earlier experiment rasterized the knowledge graph’s occurrence-derived features onto the grid and saw the lode AUC jump toward 0.97. That gain was a coverage artifact: the features and the labels were drawn from one occurrence inventory, so a cell’s own record was informing its own prediction. Under a fold-aware leave-one-out, where each held-out cell’s own record is removed from the feature set, the gain collapsed to roughly zero. Any feature derived from the occurrence inventory is treated as guilty until cleared.

Refit-on-all for the served map. The AUC numbers are held-out estimates of the pipeline’s skill. The surface that gets served is the same pipeline refit on all the labels, so it uses every occurrence to draw the best map it can. The reported AUC describes the method’s skill, not a property of the all-data refit, and the two are kept distinct.

The served surface is masked to the GeMS-mapped footprint, the only ground where the splay and intersection features are defined; outside it the favorability is not meaningful, so it is left blank. The typed lode occurrences (green) land on the high-favorability ground.

Feature importance: the Groves controls lead, ahead of the named faults

Code 
fi = gate["datasets"][0]["feature_importance_sharp_all_top12"]
names = [f[0] for f in fi][::-1]
imp = [f[1] for f in fi][::-1]
groves_feats = {"dist_splay", "dist_fault_intersection", "dist_fold_hinge"}
colors = ["#d1495b" if n in groves_feats else "#9fb1bd" for n in names]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.barh(names, imp, color=colors)
ax.set_xlabel("random-forest feature importance")
ax.set_title("Lode feature importance (top 12) — Groves controls in red")
for i, (n, v) in enumerate(zip(names, imp)):
    ax.text(v + 0.002, i, f"{v:.3f}", va="center", fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout()

The three Groves controls, splay proximity, fold-hinge distance, and fault-intersection proximity, rank as the top three features, ahead of every individually named fault and ahead of elevation. The structural law the first model failed to find was real; the first model had the wrong features for it.

The lode mirage: restriction of range, and the fix

Code 
arms = gate["datasets"][0]["arms"]
groups = ["base\n(terrain+geology\n+aeromag)", "struct_groves\n(+ Groves controls)"]
inbox = [arms["base"]["auc_placer_core"], arms["struct_groves"]["auc_placer_core"]]
district = [arms["base"]["auc_gems"], arms["struct_groves"]["auc_gems"]]

x = np.arange(len(groups)); w = 0.36
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
b1 = ax.bar(x - w/2, inbox, w, label="in-box subset (placer core)", color="#e7a33e")
b2 = ax.bar(x + w/2, district, w, label="GeMS-mapped district (the gate)", color="#2e7d6b")
ax.axhline(0.70, color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(1.45, 0.71, "0.70 gate", fontsize=8, ha="right")
ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(groups, fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("out-of-fold AUC"); ax.set_ylim(0.4, 1.0)
ax.set_title("Restriction of range: the in-box subset overstates skill")
for bars in (b1, b2):
    for r in bars:
        ax.text(r.get_x()+r.get_width()/2, r.get_height()+0.01,
                f"{r.get_height():.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=8)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()

The in-box subset (the small box around the placer core) reads high for every model, because inside it the lodes are upland schist and the background is coastal flat. That is restriction of range: the model separates the classes on the box geometry, not the geology. The GeMS-mapped district AUC is the gate that strips the geometry out. The first keyword-labeled lode model scored about 0.80 in the small box and fell to 0.58 across the district, and for a while that collapse was the chapter’s negative result. The rebuild, typed dispersed labels plus the Groves controls, brought the district number to 0.712, a +0.170 gain over the same model without the structure features, with a paired bootstrap 95% interval of +0.108 to +0.234 that clears zero.

The peninsula generalization

Code

bars = {
    "central district\n(mapped)": cen["auc_mapped"],
    "wider peninsula\n(mapped)": wid["auc_mapped"],
    "held-out east\n(Solomon/Council)": wid["auc_east"],
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
cols = ["#2e7d6b", "#2e7d6b", "#7b6cae"]
b = ax.bar(list(bars), list(bars.values()), color=cols)
ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_ylabel("out-of-fold AUC"); ax.set_ylim(0.4, 1.0)
ax.set_title("The Groves control generalizes to the wider peninsula")
for r in b:
    ax.text(r.get_x()+r.get_width()/2, r.get_height()+0.01,
            f"{r.get_height():.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"held-out east gain over base: +{wid['d_auc_east']:.3f}  "
      f"95% CI [{east_ci[0]:+.3f}, {east_ci[1]:+.3f}] (crosses zero)")
held-out east gain over base: +0.104  95% CI [-0.073, +0.282] (crosses zero)

Rebuilt on regional bedrock maps and scored on lode occurrences dispersed across the whole Seward Peninsula, the same splay-intersection-fold-host signal predicts lodes at about 0.88 on the mapped ground, and at 0.82 on an eastern cluster around Solomon and Council that the central model never trained on. The control is not a central-district artifact. The one caution is the east: with only nine eastern occurrences, the gain over the base model there is not yet distinguishable from zero (the interval crosses it), which is why the central-district surface is the served result and the peninsula extension is reported as validated but provisional.

The placer surface and the beach-line backbone

Code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
arr, ext = panel(ax, PLACER_SERVED,
                 "Served placer favorability (geomorphic terrain model)",
                 "placer favorability (RF probability)", cmap="YlGnBu",
                 mask_neg=True)
pl = placer_occ(ext)
ax.scatter(pl.geometry.x, pl.geometry.y, s=18, c="#ff2d2d", edgecolor="black",
           linewidth=0.35, label=f"placer occ (N={len(pl)})")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9)
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"placer spatial-CV AUC: {placer['mpm_geomorph_terrain_spatialCV_auc']:.3f}   "
      f"buffered: {placer['mpm_geomorph_terrain_buffered300m_auc']:.3f}   "
      f"beach-line overlay: {placer['baseline_v31_composite_auc']:.3f}")
placer spatial-CV AUC: 0.733   buffered: 0.741   beach-line overlay: 0.444

The placer surface is the one result here that held up on the first careful try. The earlier knowledge-overlay map, a hand-built picture of where the beaches run, scored 0.444 against the recorded occurrences, below a coin flip, because it is a faithful map of the coastal beaches and most of the recorded gold is up the creeks. The terrain-and-geomorphology model that learns directly from the land scored 0.733 under spatial-block cross-validation and 0.741 with a 300 m buffer. The buffered number sitting above the unbuffered one is the reassuring direction: the result is not an artifact of points leaking across fold boundaries. This surface is the placer layer goldbug serves. (The colors here use a standard high-is-bright scale; the live goldbug map applies its own styling.)

Findings

The same Nome Group veins source both maps. The lode targets are the fractured quartz-sulfide veins in the Nome Group schist; the placer gold is what weathered out of those veins and was carried down. The genesis the literature lays out is a three-stage system (the 1978 Alaska DGGS study of the Nome coastal and offshore placers): glaciers stripped the mineralized bedrock and dumped unsorted, low-grade till (about 70 ppb gold) across the coastal shelf; marine transgressions then winnowed the fine matrix out of that drift, leaving dense gold concentrated on a stack of raised and submerged beach lines; late-stage streams cut across those beaches and re-sorted them into the bonanza pay, Anvil Creek dissecting the Third Beach being the type example. That is why the placer model is a beach-line model and why the richest ground sits where streams cross old shorelines.

The negative results are signal too. Several things that looked promising did not survive the ruler, and each one rules out a feature so the next round does not re-try it:

  • Splitting the faults out by name hurt the lode model (the per-named-fault arm scored 0.422 against the lumped Groves arm’s 0.712). Orientation and structural role beat fault identity.
  • The deposit-scale Albion fault at Rock Creek was redundant once the splay and intersection bands were in (it moved the AUC by -0.021, within noise).
  • The drift-on-beach feature is data-walled: the one staged surficial map (AOF 125) does not cover the placer core, so the feature is undefined where it would matter, and a central-Nome drift vector is not yet in hand.
  • The 400 m aeromagnetics carried no independent lode signal on the flown cells (marginal AUC about -0.02 to -0.06). The DIGHEM apparent resistivity helped a little at district scale (about +0.03) but not in the central box, and neither DIGHEM layer is in the served surface. The predicted graphitic-conductor cross-check failed the other way: the graphitic units read as more resistive, not less. We did not build the combined low-magnetic / low-resistivity / gravity-low alteration index the literature advocates, so this is a limitation, not a refutation.

What each layer contributed. Terrain carries the placer model and set the trap for the first lode model. Geology supplies the host. Structure, specifically the Groves splay/intersection/fold features, is what moved the lode from chance to a real number. Of the geophysics, the magnetics did not help and the resistivity helped only marginally; structure, not geophysics, carries the lode. The typed 36a labels were half the lode fix, the Groves features the other half.
